content: Cicuta, commonly known as Water Hemlock or Cowbane, is a small genus comprising four species of highly toxic flowering plants belonging to the Apiaceae family. These plants are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with a primary distribution in North America. They are perennial herbaceous plants that can grow up to 2 meters in height. Cicuta species typically thrive in wet environments such as meadows, streambanks, and marshy areas. Although Water Hemlock bears a superficial resemblance to Poison Hemlock (genus Conium), they are distinct species despite belonging to the same botanical family. Appearance The stems of Cicuta plants are smooth, branching, and often swollen at the base. They may exhibit purple stripes or mottling, particularly in Cicuta maculata. The stems are hollow but contain partitions at the points where the leaves and stem meet. The leaves are arranged alternately and are tripinnate, with coarse, toothed edges, differing from the finely divided, lacy leaves characteristic of many other Apiaceae members. The flowers are small, white, and arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters, a hallmark of this plant family. When the stems or roots are cut, they exude an oily, yellow liquid with a strong, unpleasant odor reminiscent of parsnips, carrots, or mice. Toxicity Cicuta is extremely poisonous and is sometimes mistaken for edible plants like parsnips due to its clusters of white, tuberous roots. This misidentification can be fatal. Water Hemlock is considered by some to be the most toxic plant in North America. Ingestion of any part of the plant can result in death, often accompanied by violent and painful convulsions. While humans have succumbed to Water Hemlock poisoning throughout history, livestock are particularly vulnerable, which is why the plant is also referred to as cowbane. In livestock, death can occur within as little as 15 minutes after ingestion. The primary toxic compound in Cicuta is cicutoxin, an unsaturated aliphatic alcohol that is most concentrated in the plant's roots. In humans, symptoms typically begin within 30 to 60 minutes of ingestion and include nausea, vomiting, and tremors. These initial symptoms are followed by severe abdominal cramps, projectile vomiting, and convulsions. In some cases, long-term effects such as retrograde amnesia have been reported. Species 1. Cicuta bulbifera – Commonly known as Bulblet-bearing Water Hemlock, this species is found in northern regions of North America. 2. Cicuta douglasii – Known as Western Water Hemlock, it is native to western parts of North America. 3. Cicuta maculata – Referred to as Spotted Water Hemlock, this species is widespread across North America. 4. Cicuta virosa – Also called Cowbane or Northern Water Hemlock, it is native to northern Europe, Asia, and parts of Alaska.
